sent.t: I counted everything in my bathroom that came from the 100 yen shop.
Eight things.
13 dollars and 50 cents.
And I use every one of them, most days, and I have for years.
I am 68.
I am not thin like the women in the advertisements.
I am 5 feet tall.
I wear a size 14.
My hair went grey in my 50s and I kept it.
So when I say these eight things work, I am not saying they made me look like somebody else.
I am saying they are the things my hands reach for without thinking.
You have seen the videos, A Woman Your Age Needs Ten Steps, A Serum, An Essence, A Mist, A Patch, A Little Machine That Lights Up
Blue.
My mother dressed brides in Gion for 40 years.
She had a bowl of water, a cotton cloth and one small bottle on the shelf.
Her skin at 79 was better than mine at 40.
So the 10 steps are not the secret.
The secret is smaller and cheaper and much more boring than that.
The last thing on my list is the one nobody in America knows.
It costs $1.50.
It has been in Japanese bathrooms for a hundred years, and it is not in a bottle.
Stay with me for that one, because at the end of this you will not need to buy anything.
You will know exactly what to change tonight with what is already in your bathroom.
My name is Michiko.
I grew up in Nishijin, the weaving district of Kyoto, in the wooden house my family has had for four generations.
My mother, Fumiko, was a kitsukeshi.
She dressed brides and geiko in kimono in Gion, 40 years.
The obi tied so tight the bride could not bend.
And I lived 19 years in California, in Sunnyvale, while my husband worked in the Valley.
So I know your bathroom too.
I know the shelf under the mirror with 14 bottles on it.
I had that shelf.
I brought it home with me in 2002.
Now, 8 things in the order I would buy them again.
Number 1.
The bag of thin cotton pads.
80 of them. $1.50.
The flattest bag in the shop.
Here is the problem first.
Most of you clean your face with a cotton ball or a wipe or one of those thick pads that drinks half the bottle.
They drag.
I see women in their 60s with a red line under the eye from a cotton ball, and they think it is age.
It is cotton.
My mother never used cotton balls.
She cut squares from a soft cloth, boiled them in the kettle once a week, and kept them in a small tin by the basin.
When I came home from California in 2002 with a plastic bag of white puffs, She looked at them like they were a foreign animal.
Why this matters after 60?
The skin under your eye is thinner than a sheet of paper by now, and it does not spring back the way it did.
Whatever you put there, you should be able to put there with two fingers and no pressure at all.
A thin pad lets you do that.
A thick one makes you press.
The change is one bag, $1.50.
It lasts me two months.
Soak the pad in warm water, wring it out, then put your lotion on the pad.
Two a day.
Tonight, in the mirror.
Take the pad you use now.
Wet it.
Wipe your cheek once, slowly, and hold it under the light.
If it has lint on it, it is too fluffy for your face.
That is your check.
Number 2, the big pump bottle of lotion.
In America, you call it toner.
500ml, $2, the problem.
Women my age spend $30 on a serum and then dry their face out twice a day with a cleanser that forms like dish soap.
Then the serum cannot do anything because the skin is already tight and angry.
I saw a video last week.
A young woman with a very smooth face and she said, your skin has never been cleaner than after a double cleanse.
I thought, my mother washed brides for 40 years and she never double cleansed anything in her life.
She put warm water on a cloth and she put it on the face and she stopped.
Why it happens after 60.
Your skin makes less oil every year.
And the same cleanser you used at 45 is now too strong for you.
It is not the cleanser's fault.
It is the calendar, the change.
This bottle, two dollars, at the 100 yen shop.
I pour it into my mother's glass bottle because I like the weight of it.
But that part is free.
Three thin layers, not one thick one.
Pat, do not rub.
Wait a minute between layers.
Your face should feel like a wet peach, not a wet floor.
Tonight in the mirror, wash your face the way you always do and do not put anything on it.
Set a timer for three minutes, Then touch your cheek with the back of your fingers and smile wide and feel whether the skin pulls.
If it feels tight, your cleanser is too strong and the fix costs nothing at all.
Use half as much and rinse twice as long.
Tell me in the comments whether your face felt tight after 3 minutes.
Yui reads them to me with my tea, and I want to know how many of us are walking around with tight faces.
That little test is the most useful thing in this video.
I am serious.
Do it tonight before you buy anything.
Number 3, the konjac sponge, $1.50.
It comes hard as a piece of dried bread, and it swells up in water into something soft, the size of your palm.
My granddaughter, Yui, is 22.
She studies at Doshisha.
And three years ago, she came to the house with a plastic bag from the shop by the station.
She put a hundred little things on the tatami, and this sponge was the one she was proudest of.
She said, Grandma, you will like this one.
She was right, and I hate that she was right.
The problem.
Women over 60 scrub a washcloth, a brush, a rough towel, because scrubbing feels like doing something.
But the redness on the cheeks afterwards is not circulation, it is irritation, and it stays for an hour.
Why after 60?
The outer layer of your skin is thinner, and it takes longer to settle after a rough morning.
The sponge is the opposite of a brush.
It has no edges that change.
A dollar fifty.
Replace it every six to eight weeks and hang it where the air moves, not flat on the basin.
If it smells like a wet cellar, buy a new one.
Tonight, in the mirror, wash with whatever you use now, then look at your cheeks.
If they are pink and warm, your method is too rough.
Number four.
The small blue tube of hand cream, the one with urea on the label, $1.50.
I put one by the kitchen sink and one by the bed.
That is $3 for the pair, and I have bought this tube more times than I can count.
The problem.
Everyone spends money on the face and forgets the hands, but your hands are the first thing anyone sees of you.
You hand over money.
You shake a hand.
You hold a teacup at a table.
My mother tied obi all day in Gion, 40 years, and her hands smelled of sake and were soft as the inside of a glove.
I used to think it was luck.
It was a small tube, twice a day, for 40 years.
Why after 60?
The back of the hand has almost no oil glands.
and it is the part of you that spends the most time in water and in sun.
It goes first.
It always goes first.
The change.
A dollar fifty.
One tube by the sink, one by the bed.
And a rule I made for myself.
Put it on after every time you wash your hands, not when you remember.
Tonight, in the mirror, turn your hand over under the light and look at the knuckles.
If the skin there is white and dry, that is not the weather.
That is the answer.
Number 5, the Sake Skin Lotion, $2.
It is watery, with a memory of rice in it.
In February, the inside of this house is 35 degrees.
Wooden house, thin walls, and every February I put this on.
And I remember the winter my mother dressed a bride from a family in Fushimi, a sake family, and she came home smelling of the brewery,
and she said, Michiko, this is the smell of a good face, the problem.
Heavy cream.
In Kyoto, in July, it is 95 degrees, with the humidity of a bath, and the heavy cream sits on top of your face like a
coat you cannot take off.
Why after 60?
You do not need a thicker cream.
You need more water, in thin layers, more often.
Cream holds what you put under it.
If there is nothing under it, it holds nothing.
The change.
Two dollars.
Put it on the face, the neck, and the hands while the skin is still damp.
Then a thin cream on top, only where you need it.
The neck gets the same as the face.
Tonight, in the mirror, put your lotion on and then press the back of your hand to your cheek.
If it sticks, you have too much.
If it slides, you have the right amount.
Number 6, the 3-pack of green tea sheet masks, $2 for 3.
This one is not really about the tea.
I will be truthful about that.
My friend Carol lives in Sacramento.
She is 70.
husband passed two years ago and she calls me every Sunday night her time which is Monday morning for me and she says the same thing
at the start of every call.
Michiko, I look tired and I say Carol you are tired it is not your face the problem women my age do not stop for 10
minutes we are in the kitchen or we are on the phone or we are folding something a mask forces you to lie down that is
the whole product why after 60 the skin is not the only thing that needs the rest your face shows the week 10 minutes flat on
your back with something cool on it and the week falls off your shoulders a little the change $2 for three.
One for Sunday, when Carol calls.
One for the day after a bad night.
One for when Yui has an exam and I am nervous for her.
Tonight, in the mirror, hold the mask up to the light before you open it.
If it is dripping, squeeze it into your palm first and put that on your neck.
Do not waste the good part.
Number seven, the white cotton gloves for sleeping.
The problem.
You put cream on your hands at night, and then you cannot turn over because your hands stick to the sheet and by the second night
you have stopped putting the cream on I know I did that for years in this house in January Hiroshi sleeps in socks 30 years the
same socks the same gray cardigan in the daytime Hiroshi says the house is not cold.
It is cold, Hiroshi.
Why, after sixty, your hands lose water all night, and you cannot feel it happening?
You only see it in the morning, at the knuckles, and by then it is a week of mornings.
The change.
A dollar fifty for a pair.
Cream on, gloves on, sleep.
Wash them with the towels on Sunday and keep the second pair for the night the first pair is drying.
Tonight in the mirror.
Put the cream on, put the gloves on, go to sleep.
In the morning, before you do anything else, look at your knuckles.
That is the check and it takes one night.
If this has been useful, the button under the video is free and the subscribe button is free too and both of them help Yui keep
making these with me.
Now the last one, number eight.
This is the one, the bag of rice bran, Komenuka, a dollar fifty, and it is not in a bottle, and it is not pretty, and
it has been in Japanese bathrooms for a hundred years.
Nishijin is a weaving district.
Before the war, every house on my street had a loom, and the women who worked the looms washed their faces and their hands with the
bran from the rice they cooked that morning.
The bran went into a cloth bag, the bag went into the basin, and the bag hung by the tap until the next morning.
My mother had one.
Her mother had one.
I have one now, hanging on a hook by the window, the problem.
Foam.
You think foam is cleaning, because soap taught you that.
Foam is soap telling you it is working.
The bran does not form.
It smells like rice.
And it takes the oil off your face without taking the face with it.
Why this matters after 60?
It is gentle enough to use every single day, even on a dry face, even in February.
You can use it on your hands, your elbows, your neck, and on the back of your knees where the skin gets rough.
One bag, $1.50, one month.
The change.
Wet the bag, squeeze it a little so the milky water comes out and use that water on your face with your fingers.
No scrubbing.
Then rinse the bag and hang it up.
In summer, keep it in the refrigerator and it will feel like a small cold hand on your face in the morning.
Tonight, in the mirror, open the bag and smell it.
It smells like rice and nothing else.
If it smells like perfume, somebody has been clever with it, and you do not need clever.
You need rice.
So, eight things, $13.50, and not one of them is a Serum.
Do not go and buy all eight tonight.
Open the cupboard under your sink first and take out the bottles you have not touched since last winter.
That is the thing.
That is the whole thing.
My mother used to say, if it does not make you stand straight, it does not belong to you.
She said it about clothes.
It works for bottles too.
Now tell me something.
What is the one thing on your shelf that you have used for more than 10 years, not the newest, the one you keep buying.
Tell me in the comments and Yue will read them to me with my tea on Sunday.
And next time, Carol asks me a question I did not expect.
She asks what perfume I wear.
And my answer is going to surprise her.
See you then!
